reasons.B: Closest to Gerould's assertive, acid movement: long semicolon-joined clauses snapping into short verdicts ('I say only...'), period diction ('any one', 'neighbours'), sparing dashes and an exclamation used for scorn, and a hard-edged close.
reasons.D: Period register and balanced antithesis fit, and its rhetorical questions echo the passage, but the whimsical asides ('and then one sits down') and gentler, more hedged stance soften her bluntness.
reasons.C: Right era and some Gerould-like semicolon series, but the confiding, uneasy opening hedges too much and the parenthetical exclamation and piled-up asides tip into imitation.
reasons.A: Modern, plain, evenly paced prose with no semicolons or period diction and a measured, neutral stance; nothing of her combative early-century voice.
